title: How do tiny cloud droplets become raindrops?
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: How does a cloud make rain?

explain.say: A cloud droplet is tiny, about 0.02 millimetres across, so light that gently rising air holds it up. To fall as rain, it must grow about a hundred times wider.

draw.text: How do tiny cloud droplets become raindrops?

explain.say: In warm clouds, droplets of slightly different sizes fall at different speeds, bump into each other and merge. This is called collision and coalescence, and it slowly builds drizzle drops and then raindrops.

In cold clouds, ice crystals grow by taking vapour from the supercooled droplets around them, becoming snowflakes heavy enough to fall. They melt into raindrops on the way down; much rain outside the tropics starts this way.
One raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets' worth of water. Drops wider than about 5 millimetres wobble and break apart as they fall, so raindrops never get much bigger.

faq.a: They are so tiny that air resistance almost matches their weight; they sink only about a centimetre per second, and gentle rising air keeps them up. Only when they grow much bigger can they fall as rain.
asks: Why does a cloud not fall down?

faq.a: Droplets bump into each other and join, called coalescence, and in cold clouds ice crystals grow by taking water vapour from nearby droplets. Either way, about a million tiny droplets end up in one raindrop.
No. Small raindrops are round, and bigger ones are squashed by the air underneath into a shape like a hamburger bun. The teardrop shape is just a drawing habit.

faq.q: How big can a raindrop get?
faq.a: Most raindrops are 1 to 2 millimetres across. Drops bigger than about 5 millimetres usually break apart into smaller drops as they fall.
A typical raindrop falls at about 20 to 30 kilometres per hour, while drizzle drifts down much more slowly. Air resistance stops drops speeding up forever.
asks: What speed do raindrops fall at?

facts: A 2 millimetre raindrop holds the water of about a million cloud droplets.
The largest raindrops fall at about 9 metres per second.

quiz.say: Why are raindrops never much bigger than about 5 millimetres?
quiz.show: Raindrops stay below about 5 mm because…

options.show: Big drops break apart as they fall
options.say: Big drops break apart as they fall

quiz.why: As a big drop falls, the air flattens and wobbles it until it splits into smaller drops.

wrong.0: Storm clouds hold plenty of water; the limit comes from the drop breaking up, not a shortage.
wrong.2: Big drops evaporate more slowly than small ones, not faster.
